title: How to Scale Ad Spend Against Subliminator Production Capacity
excerpt: Doubling ad spend on a made to order store is really a production capacity question. Here is how to measure your ceiling, ramp in steps, and keep delivery promises intact while volume climbs.
body: Scaling ad spend on a print on demand store is mostly a supply question. The moment you double daily budget, the number of orders hitting production doubles with it, and a partner that handled forty orders a day comfortably can start slipping at ninety. Subliminator runs made to order production with real capacity limits, so the useful planning exercise is not how much traffic you can buy but how much production you can absorb without letting your delivery promise slip.

Start with the two numbers that actually constrain you. First, the average production time for your main product types, measured from your own order history rather than a marketing page. Second, the daily order volume at which that production time starts stretching. If your median production time is three days at forty orders a day and five days at one hundred, then the ceiling for the promise you advertise sits somewhere between those two points. Write that ceiling down before you touch a budget slider.

Then map the delivery promise you advertise to that ceiling. A store promising five to eight business days can absorb more production stretch than one promising three to five. A tight promise means your ad ramp has to be slower, or you spend the upside on refund requests and an angry inbox. A generous promise gives you room to push volume hard during a winning week. Either way the promise is the contract you made with the shopper, and capacity is what decides whether you keep it.

Ramp in steps instead of jumping. Move daily budget up by twenty to thirty percent, hold that level for three to five days, and watch production time on the orders placed during the window. If production time holds, take the next step. If it stretches, hold budget flat until the queue clears. This is slower than the spend curve most media buyers want, but it protects the thing that actually compounds: a store that delivers when it says it will earns repeat orders and reviews that make every later dollar of ad spend cheaper.

Plan the seasonal version of the same exercise in advance. Holiday periods compress production capacity across the whole industry, so the ceiling you measured in a quiet month does not apply in November. Work backwards from the last date you can still promise arrival, subtract the production and transit time you measured, and you get the final order date to advertise. Anything ordered after that needs a different promise or a different product, and telling shoppers that clearly is far cheaper than apologising to them later.

Keep one simple dashboard running through the ramp: orders placed per day, median production time, share of orders past promise, and refund rate. Those four numbers tell you within a week whether the ramp is healthy. Production time rising while refunds stay flat means you are absorbing it fine; both rising together means pull the budget back.
